synopsis: HarnessWAM organizes a LingBot-VA executor through persistent task memory, a VLM Task Manager, deterministic skill compilation, event-triggered verification, and local recovery. Its contribution is task-level orchestration around an existing WAM. The strongest ablation concerns executable-space projection: removing it reduces reported full-task success from 59.6% to 18.5%. [E03, E05, E07, E08, E10, E13]

problem.text: The authors identify a prediction–deliberation gap: finite-horizon WAM control does not itself preserve hidden scene facts, resolve targets after exploration, verify completed stages, or recover a failing multi-stage plan. Their objective is to improve global goal satisfaction through a model-external decision process that selects and verifies local WAM invocations.

contributions.text: An evidence-grounded scene belief and task graph preserve observation history, explicit uncertainty, dependencies, and unresolved entity bindings across skills.
A deterministic compiler maps semantic plans into validated WAM primitives while checking capability, arguments, dependencies, and embodiment constraints.
Progress-triggered semantic decisions coordinate skill transitions, observation requests, plan revision, and embodiment recovery within a bounded execution budget.

inputs: Global language instruction x; agent-view and wrist-view RGB observations; robot proprioceptive state q. [E03]
A benchmark-fine-tuned LingBot-VA executor, its validated primitive interface, and execution/recovery budgets. [E05, E08, E10]
outputs: Local skill instructions and continuous action chunks executed in the environment. [E03, E07]
Updated belief, evidence memory, task graph, and final verified success or failure. [E04, E07, E08]

steps.name: Maintain evidence and delayed bindings
steps.detail: Scene facts store subject, predicate, object, value, epistemic status, confidence, and supporting RGB evidence. Observed, inferred, and unknown facts remain distinct; occlusion alone does not erase established knowledge. Memory retains completed/failed nodes, retries, bindings, revisions, and salient visual evidence. Graph nodes specify operations, arguments, preconditions, effects, termination, and recovery; cognitive nodes support observation and verification alongside motor nodes.

steps.name: Compile a feasible continuation
steps.detail: Only empirically validated primitives belong to the executor's supported set. The compiler checks argument types, dependencies, precondition–effect consistency, single-arm holding state, and acyclicity. It expands supported compositions and canonicalizes instructions; infeasible plans return a failure symbol with violated constraints. Replanning preserves executed nodes and changes only the unexecuted suffix.

steps.name: Execute and monitor
steps.detail: LingBot-VA repeatedly generates action chunks for the active local instruction. A separate progress estimator reads recent dual-view frames and that instruction, predicting continuous progress, completion likelihood, and progress-bin probabilities. Milestones, exhausted skill budgets, or changed conditions/bindings trigger deliberation; progress predictions alone do not advance the graph.

steps.name: Verify and decide
steps.detail: At events, the Task Manager combines current RGB, progress history, belief, graph, evidence memory, and execution state. It labels the outcome successful, failed, or uncertain and chooses continue, advance, observe, replan, recover, or terminate. Only an advance decision completes the active motor node.

steps.name: Recover without erasing knowledge
steps.detail: Each motor node saves its initial arm and gripper state. Recovery uses multi-step joint control toward that state, clears local WAM state, preserves the environment and accumulated knowledge, and recompiles a retry or alternative continuation. Success requires all required nodes plus final visual goal verification; execution and recovery remain budget-bounded.

training.text: LingBot-VA keeps its architecture and is fine-tuned separately on each benchmark's training data. Same-WAM diagnostics and ablations share its checkpoint. Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct serves as Task Manager without task-specific fine-tuning.

The progress estimator uses five timesteps of dual-view RGB, a frozen SigLIP2-base-patch16-256 encoder, and a four-layer causal Transformer. Its six losses supervise regression, progress bins, ordering, endpoints, completion, and local monotonicity. Episodes are separated between training and validation; checkpoint selection minimizes validation progress error.

inference.text: On RoboMemArena, the WAM receives 256×256 dual-view images and robot state. The Task Manager's visual inputs contain RGB only, without depth, segmentation, or privileged simulator state. It is invoked at task events rather than every environment step.

The described harness reasons over observed execution and structured state. It does not describe candidate future-video search, inverse-dynamics action extraction, or a new learned world predictor within the Task Manager.

equations.explanation: Equation (1): the executor maps finite interaction history, proprioception, and a local skill instruction into an H-step action chunk. Selecting g_k and verifying its effects belong to the harness.

Equation (12): compilation restricts the proposed graph to plans composed of supported primitives P_W and feasible under current runtime state z_k. The implementation uses deterministic checks and expansion rules.

Equation (14): recent observations and the active instruction yield progress p_t, completion probability c_t, and a distribution over progress intervals. These are cues for semantic deliberation, not sufficient completion certificates.

results.setting: RoboMemArena: 26 tasks; 20 rollouts per task for HarnessWAM and same-WAM variants, with matched initial states, seeds, interfaces, and task budgets.
results.comparison: Static Plan: 47.9% / 62.0%; Whole Task: 44.4% / 52.3%; published PrediMem: 38.5% / 55.2%.
results.interpretation: The controlled gain over Static Plan is 11.7 / 7.9 percentage points. Full-task success requires every stage predicate; subtask success averages the completed fraction within each task. Published baselines provide context without the same checkpoint control.

results.setting: RoboCerebra Ideal, described as static and fully observable; official key-transition evaluation.
results.metric: Mean completion rate of key object-state transitions
results.interpretation: Gains are 1.78 and 2.60 percentage points. This SR measures transition completion, not the fraction of entirely successful episodes, and is not interchangeable with RoboMemArena full-task success.

results.setting: RoboMemArena with identical LingBot-VA weights, initial states, and evaluation seeds.
results.comparison: Full system: 59.6% / 69.9%; drops of 41.1 / 31.6 percentage points.
results.interpretation: This is the largest tested component removal effect. The intervention removes multiple checks together, so it establishes their combined importance rather than identifying one decisive constraint.

results.value: Reported: without task state 47.7% / 61.1%; without progress events 38.3% / 50.7%; without recovery 54.2% / 67.7%.
results.interpretation: Each intervention lowers both averages. The event ablation uses fixed-interval deliberation; the recovery ablation terminates on detected failure or budget exhaustion instead of adapting execution.

Higher partial completion accompanies lower full-task reliability. This supports evaluating global composition separately from local completion scores; it does not establish that the progress estimator is calibrated.

results.setting: Raw, normalized, and projected plans assessed using reference decompositions unavailable during inference.
results.value: Reported: raw 13.8%; normalization and aliasing 42.3%; full projection 72.9%.
results.comparison: Projection adds 30.6 percentage points beyond normalization.
results.interpretation: Lexical alignment explains part of the improvement, while further constraints improve the diagnostic substantially. Offline executability is distinct from executed task success.

limitations.text: The authors leave real-world manipulation, broader WAM skill repertoires, and calibrated uncertainty-aware deliberation to future work. These benchmark results therefore do not establish physical deployment reliability.

The paper reports matched same-WAM trials but no confidence intervals or dispersion. Published-baseline comparisons also change the underlying systems; they provide weaker attribution than the controlled diagnostics.
State removal combines belief, history, and binding removal; projection removal combines several compiler checks. Their individual contributions and interactions remain unresolved.

The fixed-interval event ablation lacks a specified invocation interval, call-count comparison, or latency measurement. Its success gap does not establish a compute-matched advantage or quantify runtime efficiency.

Recovery restores robot configuration while preserving changed object states. It cannot be assumed to undo failed manipulation; collision avoidance and recovery reliability after irreversible scene changes are not established.

reproduction.text: Reproduction requires benchmark-specific LingBot-VA checkpoints, Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct, the progress estimator, and the matched evaluation protocol. WAM fine-tuning hyperparameters, data quantities, action horizon, numerical execution budgets, and hardware requirements are not specified in the supplied implementation account.

The validated primitive registry, validation procedure, compiler rules, Task Manager prompts, progress-label construction, numerical loss weights, event thresholds, and recovery-controller settings need implementation-level clarification. Equation (15) also repeats λ_r for regression and ranking without explaining whether that sharing is intentional.

A focused reproduction would compare normalization alone against full projection using the same generated plans and fixed WAM checkpoint. Measure offline plan validity and executed task success separately under matched budgets; this directly tests the mechanism most strongly implicated by the reported diagnostics.

reasoning.text: The WAM and Dual-system labels are supported by the separation of a LingBot-VA executor from the VLM Task Manager and external runtime. Persistent task state supports Memory & long-horizon modeling. Other mechanisms and Outside quadrants fit the proposed orchestration mechanism, which adds neither joint future/action prediction nor inverse dynamics. However, Policy post-training & WM-RL is not clearly established as a contribution: benchmark fine-tuning is reported, but no new policy post-training algorithm or RL procedure is described. Without a definition admitting routine fine-tuning, the complete snapshot cannot be verified.

discussionQuestions: Which compiler constraints retain the largest execution benefit after every variant receives identical lexical normalization? [E13, E15]
Does progress-triggered deliberation outperform fixed-interval verification when VLM call counts and wall-clock budgets are matched? [E06, E13]
When failed actions alter object poses, how should recovery update feasibility while preserving useful historical evidence? [E04, E08]

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, title, author list, and arXiv footer
evidence.detail: The title and all eleven catalog authors agree with the supplied title page. The footer identifies arXiv:2608.09516v1, dated 10 August 2026.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 1–3, Abstract, Section 1, and Section 2.1
evidence.detail: The authors motivate persistent deliberation beyond local predictive control and position HarnessWAM as a runtime external to an existing WAM.
The formulation specifies dual-view RGB, proprioception, local instructions, action chunks, and a harness state containing belief, graph, memory, and skill execution state.
Facts carry epistemic status and evidence; memory stores task history and visuals. Graphs contain dependencies, partial entity bindings, and motor/cognitive nodes with execution semantics.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 5–6, Section 3.3, Equations (9)–(13) and compiler description
evidence.detail: Supported primitives require validated WAM realizations. Deterministic compilation enforces types, dependencies, holding state, preconditions/effects, and acyclicity, while revisions preserve executed history.

The progress estimator predicts progress, completion, and bins with six training objectives. Milestones, budgets, and condition changes trigger deliberation; progress alone never advances the graph. The displayed loss repeats λ_r.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Algorithm 1 and Section 3.4, Equation (16)
evidence.detail: The inference loop executes actions and gathers observations. Task Manager outputs include outcome labels, six decision types, belief/binding updates, and revision requests; advance marks an active motor node complete.

evidence.location: PDF p. 8, Section 3.5, Equation (17), and Section 3.6
evidence.detail: Recovery targets saved arm/gripper state, preserves environment and memory, and clears local WAM state. Goal verification and bounded task-level execution/recovery govern termination.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 8–9, Section 4.1, Benchmarks, Metrics, Equations (18)–(20), and Evaluation protocol
evidence.detail: RoboMemArena has 26 tasks. Full-task success requires all stage predicates; subtask and RoboCerebra SR average completed predicates/transitions. HarnessWAM and same-WAM variants use 20 rollouts per task with matched conditions.

evidence.location: PDF p. 9, Section 4.1, Models and implementation details and Baselines
evidence.detail: LingBot-VA is fine-tuned per benchmark and shared within controlled comparisons. The paper specifies Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct, RGB restrictions, 256×256 WAM images, five-frame progress inputs, frozen SigLIP2, a four-layer temporal Transformer, and episode-level validation.

evidence.location: PDF p. 10, Table 1, Average SRtask/SRsub columns, and Section 4.2 RoboMemArena
evidence.detail: Average pairs are HarnessWAM 59.6/69.9, Static Plan 47.9/62.0, Whole Task 44.4/52.3, and PrediMem 38.5/55.2, all percentages.

evidence.location: PDF p. 10, Table 2, Ideal SR column, and Section 4.2 RoboCerebra
evidence.detail: Ideal SR is 23.70% for HarnessWAM, 21.92% for GPT-4o Planner + OpenVLA, and 21.10% for HPE. The prose describes Ideal as static and fully observable.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 10–11, Section 4.3 intervention descriptions; Table 3, Average columns; Task-level effects
evidence.detail: Full-task/subtask percentages are 59.6/69.9 for the full system, 47.7/61.1 without state, 18.5/38.3 without projection, 38.3/50.7 without progress events, 55.4/68.4 with progress-only switching, and 54.2/67.7 without recovery.

evidence.location: PDF p. 11, Table 3, Sequence columns, and Task-level effects paragraph on progress-only switching
evidence.detail: Sequential-execution full-task/subtask success is 86.3/93.0% for HarnessWAM and 72.5/97.9% with progress-only switching; the prose explicitly confirms the contrast.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 11–12, Table 4 and Plan-level diagnosis of executable-space projection
evidence.detail: Executability rises from 13.8% for raw plans to 42.3% after normalization and 72.9% after full projection. Reference decompositions support offline analysis and are not supplied during inference.
The conclusion identifies real-world manipulation, broader WAM skill repertoires, and calibrated uncertainty-aware deliberation as future directions.
